s: Part six.
Provenance and uncertainty.
By the end of this part, you'll know how to keep every claim tied to its source, what to do when sources disagree, and where the platform's citation feature helps and where it stops.
Let's start with a picture.
A colleague tells you the deadline is the fifteenth.
If it matters, you have two choices.
Trust them.
Or go and check yourself.
Now suppose they say this instead.
The fifteenth, from procurement's email on Tuesday, third paragraph.
Checking takes twenty seconds.
The claim did not become more true.
It became cheap to verify.
And that is the difference between a summary that saves you work, and a summary that just moves the work somewhere else.
In exam terms, synthesis without provenance is unverifiable.
And unverifiable output makes the reviewer redo the work.
Think about it.
A system reads six sources and produces one fluent paragraph.
The only way to check it is to read all six.
So the system saved nobody anything.
A claim-to-source mapping changes that.
It converts review from re-derivation into spot-checking.
The notes name four parts of provenance.
And the exam expects you to know all four.
First.
Claim-to-source mapping.
Each assertion is tied to the specific source and location that supports it.
Not a bibliography at the end.
Second.
Temporal handling.
When each source was retrieved, and what date or period it describes.
Why?
Because two sources that disagree may both be right, about different dates.
Third.
Conflict annotation.
Surfacing disagreement, instead of resolving it silently.
Fourth.
Coverage gaps.
Stating what was not found, so absence of evidence is not read as evidence of absence.
What does it look like concretely?
Two linked lists.
The first is a claims list.
Each claim has an ID, its text, and the IDs of the sources supporting it.
The second is a sources list.
Each source has an ID, a title, a locator such as a section and page, a verbatim quote, a retrieved-at timestamp, and an effective date.
The shared source ID is the link.
And here's the rule the exam tests.
A step that consumes structured findings and outputs only prose breaks the chain.
Hold on to this line.
Render the prose from the arrays, not instead of them.
Question one.
Here's the scenario.
A pipeline extracts figures from an annual report, two quarterly filings, and an analyst note.
It puts them into records that each carry a source ID and a page.
Then a final merge step writes one company-profile paragraph for credit analysts.
The analysts cannot tell which filing a revenue figure came from.
So they end up re-reading all four.
Where did it go wrong, and what's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
The provenance existed, and it broke at the merge step.
So have the merge step output claims and sources arrays, linked by source ID, with a quote and page per claim.
And render the prose from them.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: append a bibliography of the four documents.
Why?
It lists what was read.
But not which source supports which claim.
Wrong: write "according to the filings" beside each figure.
Why?
That's vague attribution.
It isn't verifiable.
Wrong: add an overall confidence rating.
Why?
It tells the analyst nothing about where a figure came from.
So, bibliography versus claim mapping.
A bibliography answers "what did you read?"
A claim mapping answers "where does this particular number come from?"
Only the second saves the reviewer time.
Takeaway.
Every claim keeps a link to its source, with a quote and a location, all the way to the final prose.
The second concept is what to do when the sources disagree.
And here the exam's answer is, at first hearing, a refusal to answer.
The plain version.
A colleague is asked for a deadline, and finds two emails with different dates.
The helpful reply goes like this.
Procurement says the fifteenth.
Finance says the twentieth.
The finance email is newer, but may cover a different step, so someone needs to confirm.
And I found nothing about the Asia office.
That reply doesn't pick a winner.
It hands you a decision you can make in two minutes.
In exam terms.
When sources conflict, and there is no basis for choosing, any single figure is wrong as an output.
Why?
Because it hides the fact that there is no one answer.
So what does the output carry?
One.
Both claims, with their quotes, locators, retrieval times, and effective dates.
Two.
A conflict annotation.
That names which claims are in tension, and the nature of the disagreement.
It gives a temporal note explaining it, if dates are involved.
It states explicitly that this agent did not resolve it.
And it gives a reviewer action, naming the specific question a human must settle.
Three.
An explicit unresolved status on the answer.
The notes use conflicted_unresolved.
Four.
A list of coverage gaps.
This is the principle from the earlier chapters.
Give the model a truthful way to say "I do not know," rather than forcing a choice between a fabrication and a format violation.
Question two.
This one is select two.
Here's the scenario.
A research system is asked for the size of the battery-recycling market.
One subagent cites a twenty twenty-four industry report, at twelve billion dollars.
Another cites a twenty twenty-six government release, at nine billion, under a narrower definition.
Nothing settles which definition the requester means.
And no data was found for Southeast Asia.
Which two elements belong in the output?
Take a second.
The answers.
First.
Both claims, with quote, locator, retrieval time and source date.
Plus an unresolved conflict annotation, naming the human decision needed.
Second.
A coverage-gap statement that no Southeast Asia data was found.
So the absence is not read as a zero market.
Now the wrong turns.
They're three different ways of resolving the conflict silently.
Wrong: report the newer figure, and footnote the older as superseded.
Why?
Recency is a heuristic about currency, not evidence about which source governs.
And here the definitions differ too.
Wrong: search for more reports, and take whichever figure most sources support.
Why?
Agreement among retrieved sources is not authority.
Adding sources to a definitional dispute produces a vote, not an answer.
Wrong: average the two into a blended estimate.
Why?
That's a number neither source supports.
It hides the disagreement behind a confident blend.
The notes' own worked example is a data retention question.
A named governing policy, from twenty twenty-four, says seven years.
A finance records schedule, from twenty twenty-six, citing a regulatory update, says ten.
Why not just return the newer figure?
Because the older document is the named authority in the policy register.
And the newer one may not have the power to change it.
The real finding is that the organisation's documents are out of sync.
A confident "ten years" would have hidden that control gap.
Possibly for years.
And the same scenario shows why gating on stated confidence fails.
The problematic answer was already high confidence.
So a check that rejects low confidence would never have fired.
Takeaway.
When sources conflict, show both, explain the dates, name the decision a human must make, and say what you did not find.
The last concept is what the platform does for you.
And where it stops.
The plain version.
A reporter can footnote quotes from published reports, with page numbers.
For a fact learned in a phone call, there is no page.
So the reporter logs who said it, when, and the call reference.
Both kinds of fact need a trail.
Just a different kind of trail.
In exam terms, the Citations feature is enabled per document.
You set citations, with enabled set to true, on that document in the request.
The API then returns citation objects attached to the answer text.
Each one carries three things.
cited_text, which is the exact source passage.
A document_index.
And a location.
That's char_location for plain text, or page_location for PDF documents.
The documentation, as the notes record it, says three more things.
The API parses citations into valid pointers.
That improves citation quality over asking the model to write references itself.
And cited_text does not count toward output tokens.
Where citations don't apply, for example when synthesising across tool results rather than documents, you carry provenance in your own record structure.
The tool name.
The record ID.
And the retrieval time.
Question three.
Here's the scenario.
A support knowledge assistant combines policy PDFs with live results from an order-management tool.
Compliance requires every statement to be traceable to its exact source.
Citations are enabled on the policy documents only.
What else is needed?
Take a second.
The answer.
Carry provenance for the tool-derived statements in the team's own records.
Tool name, record ID, retrieval time.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: nothing more is needed, because the citations will cover the tool results too.
Why?
Citations point into the documents they were enabled on.
Wrong: instruct the model to write a page number after every statement.
Why?
That's less reliable than parsed pointers.
And it's meaningless for a tool result, which has no page.
Wrong: paste the full cited policy pages into the answer.
Why?
It bloats the answer, without mapping any statement to its passage.
One honest caveat.
The notes say Citations cover supplied documents, not tool results.
That reflects the documentation when the notes were written.
Product behaviour may have moved since.
Don't let that distract you.
The exam point is not a feature boundary.
It's that every claim-to-source mapping stays intact, whichever mechanism carries it.
If a question tells you a statement has no citation pointer, the answer is to carry its provenance yourself.
And one last contrast for this part.
Confidence versus sources.
A confidence rating tells a reviewer how sure the system claims to be.
A source tells the reviewer how to check.
When an option offers a confidence label as the fix for a provenance problem, it is the wrong answer every time.
That's part six.
If you remember one thing, make it this.
Use citations for documents, your own provenance records for tool results, and never let a merge step drop the link.
Coming up: the trap round.
Rapid fire, across the whole chapter.
The trap round.
Rapid fire.
I'll say the thing you might see in an answer option.
Then what you should think.
We'll go in the order of the parts.
First, long conversations.
If you see a bigger context window as the fix for a long session going wrong, think density and placement, not capacity.
The failure comes back later.
If you see more output tokens, think wrong budget.
It changes what the model can write, not what it is reading.
If you see instruct the summariser to keep the important numbers, think a lossy summary with better odds.
Pin the facts in a block, or persist them.
If you see a facts block filled from what the customer said, think right structure, wrong source.
Tool-verified values only.
Still on long conversations.
If you see clearing old tool results, think gone, not blurred, and no pointer back.
If you see compaction for identifiers, think identifiers degrade first.
If you see raise the compaction trigger, think delay, not prevention.
If you see disable compaction, think hard overflow.
If you see "the logs must stay auditable," think trim at the hook and keep the raw-output path.
If you see "the agent keeps reverting" after a phase change, think fresh session with a handoff brief.
Where anything left out is gone.
If you see documents placed after the question, think backwards.
Bulk first, question last.
If you see a hard constraint buried in the middle, think move it, and also check it in code.
Next, escalation.
If you see escalation on sentiment, complexity, or a one-to-ten self-rating, think unreliable proxy.
Escalate on checkable criteria.
If you see an escalation quota, think arbitrary.
And it can suppress a real hard case.
If you see a customer asking for a human and a high automation success rate, think the success rate is irrelevant.
Escalate now.
If you see guess the most likely order, think confident wrong action.
If you see ask for four fields, think interrogation.
One question, then a human.
If you see two playbooks in conflict, and an option to ask the customer to choose, think policy gap.
Abstain, attach both, review weekly.
If you see a holding reply saying it has been approved, think prohibited.
Next, errors between agents.
If you see an empty result with status success after a timeout, think not searched is not nothing found.
If you see retry until at least one result, or raise the retry limit on a four-oh-three, think classification overrides the counter.
If you see each subagent with its own error labels, or a translation table, think one vocabulary.
Transient, business, permission.
With detail in error_code.
If you see lower the confidence or add a caveat as the fix for a coverage gap, think name the gap.
How many of how many, and which ones.
If you see the coordinator re-read or redo the subagent's work, think full cost twice.
Fix the return contract.
Next, codebase exploration.
If you see a subagent return "looks mostly fine," think the trip was wasted.
Files, line ranges, the finding, the test, what was not examined.
If you see a bigger model for the subagent, think a more fluent impression.
Still no line numbers.
If you see read the likely directories first, preload recent files, or concatenate the repository, think search, then read the matched ranges.
If you see split the files into batches in separate sessions, think no batch can see the others.
Next, review and confidence.
If you see a threshold chosen because it sounds right, or ninety-five percent on a random sample, think calibrate.
On a labelled, stratified sample, per type, against a stated target.
If you see a higher global threshold, think still uncalibrated, and costlier everywhere.
If you see average stated confidence as the error rate, think confidently wrong items are invisible to it.
If you see the model justify its own score, or extended thinking to ground confidence, think same process, no measurement.
If you see three runs agree, so approve, think shared blind spots agree too.
If you see a random sample as the only control for regulated output, think sampling measures.
It does not gate.
And last, provenance.
If you see a bibliography, "according to the sources," or an overall confidence rating as provenance, think claim-level mapping, with quote and locator.
If you see newest source wins, majority vote, or an average of two figures, think silent resolution.
Show both, mark it unresolved, name the human decision.
If you see citations assumed to cover tool results, think your own provenance record.
Tool, record ID, retrieval time.
That's the trap round.
Notice how many of those wrong answers were a global remedy.
A bigger memory, a retry, a higher threshold, more sources.
Coming up: the closing recap.
Ten things to remember.
The closing recap.
Ten things to remember from chapter five.
For each one, I'll give you the plain idea first, then the technical name.
First.
The model rereads everything every turn.
So memory is luggage you pay for on every trip.
And a bigger bag is not a plan.
The technical name is the context window as a budget, with context rot as the silent limit.
Second.
Pin the facts that matter at the top.
And only facts a tool confirmed.
That is the case-facts block, refreshed each turn.
Third.
Cut the noise out of tool output before it piles up, and keep a pointer to the original.
That is trimming at the post-tool-use hook, with a raw-output path.
Fourth.
Write down names, numbers and file locations the moment you find them, because summaries lose them first.
That is extract before you clear, persist before you summarise.
Compaction and clearing are both lossy, in different ways.
Fifth.
Put the bulk first and the question last.
And when the history has turned against you, start again with a careful one-page brief.
That is placement against the lost-in-the-middle tendency, and a fresh session with a handoff brief.
Sixth.
Fetch a human for reasons you can point to in the record.
Give a human to anyone who asks.
Ask at most one clarifying question.
And file policy holes instead of guessing.
That is checkable escalation criteria, an explicit-request hard trigger, a one-question clarification budget, and a policy-gap abstention path reviewed weekly.
Seventh.
When part of a job fails, say exactly which part, what kind of failure, and whether trying again could help.
And carry that all the way to the person reading the report.
That is a structured partial result with error_class, error_code, retryable, coverage counts and claim_scope.
And no laundering by the coordinator.
Eighth.
To explore a big codebase, search first, and read only what the search points to.
And when you send a helper, tell them exactly what to bring back.
That is search-then-read, just-in-time retrieval, and a subagent return contract.
Ninth.
A confidence number means nothing until you have counted it against real outcomes, separately for each kind of input.
And the three kinds of review do three different jobs.
That is calibration on a labelled, stratified sample with per-segment thresholds.
Plus thresholding, stratified auditing and full review, running together with a feedback loop.
Tenth.
Every claim keeps its link to the source.
Conflicts are shown rather than settled.
And what you did not find is part of the answer.
That is claim-to-source mapping, temporal handling, conflict annotation with an unresolved status, and coverage gaps.
Using Citations for documents, and your own records for tool results.
That is domain five.
Fifteen percent of the exam.
And almost all of it comes down to one habit.
When something goes wrong, find the actual cause.
And prefer the fix that costs less, for the same reliability.
